item.title: [Marketing 101 #8] Why Your $4.99 Coffee Isn't Really About the Coffee
item.body:
> Price is the only part of marketing that brings money in — everything else spends it. This lesson covers how prices get set, why $9.99 feels cheaper than $10, and how the same seat on the same flight can cost three different amounts.

## 오늘의 개념

Most people think pricing is arithmetic: add up your costs, tack on a profit, done. That's one real method, but it's the least interesting one.

There are three broad ways companies land on a number.

**Cost-based pricing.** Start with what it costs you to make the thing, add a markup. A restaurant that spends $4 on ingredients and wants a 70% food-cost margin lands near $13. It's simple and safe, and it has a blind spot: your costs are none of the customer's business. If nobody wants the dish at $13, the math doesn't care.

**Competition-based pricing.** Look at what everyone else charges and position yourself against it — matching, slightly under, or deliberately above. Gas stations do this in near-real time. The risk is that you outsource your strategy to your rivals, and if they're wrong, so are you.

**Value-based pricing.** Start at the other end: what is this worth to the buyer? A $200 pair of prescription glasses and a $600 pair may cost nearly the same to produce. The gap is what the buyer believes about the frame. This is the method most marketers push toward, because it starts with the customer instead of the spreadsheet.

Then there's the second layer: **psychological pricing** — how the number *reads*, not just what it is.

- *Charm pricing*: $9.99 instead of $10. Research generally shows a small but real lift in demand, mostly because we read left to right and anchor on the "9." The effect is modest and works best on value-driven, everyday purchases.
- *Prestige pricing*: a round $500 rather than $499. For luxury goods, a clean number signals confidence; the discount cue would undercut the product.
- *Anchoring*: showing a $1,200 laptop next to a $799 one makes the $799 feel reasonable. The first number you see sets the mental yardstick.
- *Decoy effect*: small popcorn $4, large $8 feels like a stretch — until a medium appears at $7.50 and the large suddenly looks like a bargain. The medium isn't there to sell; it's there to make the large look good.

The third layer: **price discrimination** — charging different buyers different prices for essentially the same thing. It sounds shady, and the name doesn't help, but it's usually legal and often makes everyone better off. Economists sort it into three degrees:

- *First degree*: a custom price per customer. Rare in retail, common in car dealerships and B2B contracts.
- *Second degree*: the price depends on **what you choose** — size, tier, or quantity. Costco bulk packs, Spotify Free vs. Premium, a coffee shop's 12/16/20 oz cups. Customers sort themselves.
- *Third degree*: the price depends on **who you are** — student, senior, or military discounts; regional pricing.

The unifying idea: different people are willing to pay different amounts, and a single price either leaves money on the table or leaves customers behind. Price discrimination lets a seller capture more of both ends.

One legal note worth knowing: charging different prices to different *consumers* is generally fine in the U.S. The Robinson-Patman Act restricts price discrimination between *competing business buyers* of the same commodity, and antitrust law prohibits *price fixing* — competitors agreeing on prices. Those are different things from a senior discount.

## 일상 속에서

Book a flight from Chicago O'Hare to Denver and you'll see all three layers in one screen.

The airline doesn't price by cost. Once the plane is flying, the marginal cost of one more passenger is roughly the fuel for their body weight and a can of soda — call it $30. Yet fares range from $89 to $450 on the same aircraft on the same Tuesday. That's **value-based pricing** meeting **price discrimination**.

Who's paying $450? The consultant booking Monday morning, returning Thursday night, who booked eight days out. Who's paying $89? The traveler who booked seven weeks ahead, flies Tuesday to Saturday, and doesn't mind a middle seat in the back. The airline never asks "are you a business traveler?" — it doesn't have to. It builds fences: advance-purchase requirements, Saturday-night stays, change fees. Business travelers won't jump those fences, so they sort themselves into the expensive fare. That's textbook second-degree discrimination.

Now look at the seat map. Basic Economy at $89, Main Cabin at $129, Comfort+ at $189. Most travelers don't pick Basic — it doesn't allow a carry-on or seat selection. It exists largely to make $129 feel like the sensible middle. **Decoy effect**, in the wild.

And the fare reads $129, not $130. **Charm pricing**, doing its small quiet work.

Compare that to a Delta One transcontinental seat listed at $1,200 — a clean round number. Nobody spending four figures on a lie-flat seat wants to see $1,199. **Prestige pricing** takes over where charm pricing stops working.

Same plane. Same route. Same day. Four pricing concepts stacked in a single booking screen.

## 3줄 정리

1. Prices are set three ways — from costs, from competitors, or from customer value — and value-based pricing is usually the most profitable because it starts with the buyer, not the spreadsheet.
2. Psychological pricing shapes how a number is read: $9.99 for everyday value, a round $500 for luxury, and decoys or anchors to make the target option look reasonable.
3. Price discrimination charges different buyers different amounts for nearly the same product, using self-selection (tiers, sizes, advance purchase) or identity (student, senior) — and it's how one plane carries $89 and $450 passengers at once.

## ✅ 셀프 퀴즈

**1.** A boutique sells a handmade leather bag. The materials and labor cost $80. The owner researches what customers say the bag is worth to them and prices it at $340. Which pricing method is this?

- A) Cost-based pricing
- B) Competition-based pricing
- C) Value-based pricing
- D) Penetration pricing

**2.** A movie theater offers popcorn at Small $4.00, Medium $7.50, and Large $8.00. The medium size sells poorly, but the theater keeps it on the menu anyway. What is the medium most likely doing?

- A) Acting as a decoy that makes the Large look like better value
- B) Covering the fixed cost of the popcorn machine
- C) Serving as an example of charm pricing
- D) Preventing price fixing among competing theaters

**3.** O/X: Offering a discounted movie ticket to customers over 65 is a form of third-degree price discrimination.

## 📚 오늘의 용어

- **Cost-based pricing** — Setting a price by starting from production cost and adding a markup or target margin.
- **Value-based pricing** — Setting a price from what the product is worth to the customer, independent of what it cost to make.
- **Charm pricing** — Ending a price just below a round number (e.g., $9.99) so it reads as meaningfully cheaper.
- **Anchoring** — The tendency to judge a price against the first number encountered, which becomes a mental reference point.
- **Price discrimination** — Charging different buyers different prices for essentially the same product, based on what they choose (second degree) or who they are (third degree).

---

*정답: 1 → C. The owner ignores the $80 cost and prices from perceived customer worth — that's value-based pricing. (A would have set a fixed markup on the $80; B would have matched rival boutiques.) 2 → A. A poorly selling middle option that makes the adjacent premium option look like a bargain is a decoy; the $0.50 gap between Medium and Large makes the Large nearly irresistible. 3 → O. Third-degree price discrimination sets prices by observable customer group — age, student status, region — which is exactly what a senior discount does. Note that a "large vs. small popcorn" price gap would be second degree, since the customer self-selects by choosing a size.*
